title: Scenario catalogue
Trials and other designs
text: In a randomised trial the investigator assigns the intervention by chance. Randomisation makes the arms comparable in everything, measured or not, so a difference in outcomes is caused by the intervention or by chance, and the confidence interval accounts for chance. There is no confounding to adjust for at baseline. What remains can still bias a trial: who leaves it, who does not take the treatment, and how the outcome is measured. This page covers the trial designs, then two designs that are not trials but look like them (before-after, method comparison), and diagnostic accuracy studies.

title: Trials and other designs
text:
Parallel randomised trial





















Figure 1: A parallel trial. The comparison that keeps the protection of randomisation is by assigned arm: intention to treat (ITT).



Estimates. The effect of being assigned the intervention, as risk difference, risk ratio, NNT, odds ratio, hazard ratio or mean difference.
Strengths. Randomisation removes confounding, known and unknown; blinding removes bias in measuring the outcome and in co-interventions; the strongest evidence for an effect.
Limitations. Expensive; selected participants and strict protocols (results may not apply to every patient); short follow-up; impossible or unethical for harmful exposures. Non-adherence dilutes the intention-to-treat effect, and the alternatives are no longer randomised comparisons: as treated (by the treatment received) and per protocol (only those who followed it) are confounded by whatever made people stop (Hernán and Robins 2017). Losses to follow-up related to prognosis bias any analysis.
Analysis. Binary outcome: risks per arm, RD with NNT, RR (Frequencies ▸ Independent Samples), or logistic regression. Continuous: difference in means (t-test), or ANCOVA adjusted for the baseline value, which is more precise. Time to event: Kaplan-Meier and Cox. Adjusting for strong prognostic factors increases precision. For odds and hazard ratios it also changes the estimand, from marginal to conditional (Measures and models).
Interpretation. “Risk of pancreatitis 17% with placebo and 9% with indomethacin: 8 fewer cases per 100 patients treated, NNT 12.” The odds ratio of the crude comparison is the effect on the population of patients, not on an individual with given characteristics.

title: Trials and other designs
text:
Cluster randomised trial





















Figure 2: Twelve clusters (villages, schools, practices) randomised as a whole. People in a cluster resemble each other, so the trial has less information than its number of people suggests.



What it is. Groups are randomised: villages, schools, wards. Necessary when the intervention acts on groups (hand-washing campaigns, a new ward protocol) or when individuals would contaminate each other.
Strengths. Feasible for community interventions; avoids contamination.
Limitations. Outcomes of people in the same cluster are correlated (the intraclass correlation, ICC), so the effective sample size is smaller: the design effect is 1 + (m − 1) × ICC for clusters of m people. Few clusters means chance imbalance between arms.
Analysis. A mixed (multilevel) model with a random intercept per cluster (GAMLj), or cluster-robust standard errors. Ignoring the clusters gives confidence intervals that are too narrow.
Interpretation. A mixed logistic model gives an odds ratio within clusters (conditional); a model with robust errors gives the population-average one, which is closer to 1.
In studysim. Handwashing and childhood pneumonia (counts of pneumonia), Vitamin A and child mortality, cluster randomised trial; vary the intraclass correlation.

title: Trials and other designs
text:
2×2 factorial trial
Two interventions randomised independently, so each participant gets one of four combinations. One trial answers two questions, if the interventions do not interact: each main effect is estimated by comparing everyone with and without it. With an interaction the main effects are averages over the other intervention, and the trial needs to be powered to detect the interaction. Analyse with both treatments in the model (ANOVA, logistic or Cox regression) and test their product term. In studysim: Aspirin and beta-carotene in male physicians (aspirin and beta-carotene).

title: Trials and other designs
text:
Crossover trial





















Figure 3: A 2×2 crossover: each participant receives both treatments, in a random order, separated by a washout.



What it is. Each participant receives both treatments in random order, for stable chronic conditions and treatments whose effect wears off.
Strengths. Each participant is their own control: with outcomes that are correlated within a person, far fewer participants are needed.
Limitations. Only for reversible effects and stable conditions; a carryover effect of the first treatment into the second period biases the comparison; dropouts lose both periods.
Analysis. Paired t-test of the outcome under A and under B (one row per person: Repeated measures: wide), or a mixed model with treatment and period as fixed effects and the participant as cluster (long layout), which also estimates the period effect.
In studysim. Antihypertensive drug or Bioequivalence of two formulations, 2×2 crossover; Design options ▸ period and carryover effects.

title: Trials and other designs
text:
Longitudinal trial





















Figure 4: Sixty children of a simulated longitudinal trial (Succimer for lead-exposed children), with 25% dropout: thin lines are children (some stop early), thick lines the mean of those still seen at each visit.



Repeated visits give the trajectory of the effect, but participants drop out, and dropout usually depends on how they were doing. Comparing only the completers at the last visit is biased when dropout depends on earlier values. A linear mixed model with all visits (random intercept per participant, treatment by visit) is valid when dropout depends on values already observed (missing at random). jamovi: GAMLj Mixed Models; repeated-measures ANOVA uses completers only.

title: Trials and other designs
text:
Before-after study (no control group)





















Figure 5: Regression to the mean. Nobody is treated, but people enrolled because their first value was high (above the vertical line) have lower values when measured again: part of a high value was chance, and chance does not repeat.



Everyone is measured before and after the intervention. The mean change mixes the effect with the natural course of the condition, with what else happened meanwhile and, when people are enrolled because their values were high, with regression to the mean (Barnett 2005). A paired t-test tests the change, not the effect. A control group (a trial) is the remedy; failing that, enrol on a separate baseline measurement or repeat it. In studysim: Metformin vs placebo on HbA1c, before-after, with Enrol only above percentile.

title: Trials and other designs
text:
Diagnostic accuracy study





















Figure 6: A marker that is higher in people with the disease. At a cut-off (dashed), the shaded area of the diseased is the sensitivity and that of the non-diseased one minus the specificity; moving the cut-off traces the ROC curve.



What it is. A sample of people in whom the test would be used, all receiving the index test and the reference standard (the best available way of knowing who has the disease).
Estimates. Sensitivity and specificity at a cut-off, the ROC curve and its area (AUC), likelihood ratios, and the predictive values (PPV, NPV), which also depend on the prevalence.
Biases. Spectrum bias: studying severe cases and healthy volunteers instead of the patients where the test is needed overstates accuracy (Ransohoff and Feinstein 1978). Partial verification: when only test-positives (and some negatives) get the reference standard, sensitivity is overstated and specificity understated. An imperfect reference standard, and a cut-off chosen on the same data, flatter the test.
Analysis. 2×2 table at a cut-off; ROC analysis (meddecide, psychoPDA); logistic regression to combine markers, validated on other data.
In studysim. PSA and prostate cancer, High-sensitivity troponin for myocardial infarction, diagnostic design; Biases ▸ spectrum and verification.

title: Trials and other designs
text:
Method comparison
Two methods measure the same quantity in the same people (a new device against the standard). A correlation coefficient says nothing about agreement: two methods can correlate perfectly and differ by 10 units. The Bland-Altman analysis plots the difference against the mean of the two and reports the mean difference (bias) and the limits of agreement, mean ± 1.96 SD of the differences, within which 95% of the differences fall (Martin Bland and Altman 1986). Whether those limits are acceptable is a clinical decision. A slope in the plot shows a proportional bias.





















Figure 7: Bland-Altman plot of two simulated blood pressure devices (Blood pressure in US adults, method comparison): method B reads 9.5 mmHg lower on average, and the sloping line shows that the gap grows with the pressure (proportional bias).

title: Simulated study
text: Simulate ▸ Simulated study builds one study and opens its data.

title: Simulated study
text:
Scenario, outcome and design



The options panel.



Scenarios for design narrows the pickers to the scenarios (and outcomes) that fit one design, e.g. every scenario that can be run as a case-cohort study.
Scenario and Outcome come from the library (built-in, or a custom one read with Browse…), grouped by clinical domain.
Design lists only the designs that fit the outcome: an event in a population can be studied with a cohort or a case-control study (unmatched or matched), a patient outcome with a prognosis cohort, a treatment effect with a randomised trial or, for continuous outcomes, a 2×2 crossover.
Variables: every variable is measured at start; untick one to leave it out of the dataset. It still acts on the outcome, which is how you teach residual confounding. The second column shows units or categories; the Exposure column marks the variable(s) the biases act on (below).
Form groups a numeric variable: median split, tertiles, quartiles, quintiles (cut points from the sample, as a study would compute them) or cuts typed as values (18.5, 25, 30; with a decimal comma 18,5; 25) or percentiles (10%, 90%). Labels read Q2: 120–131 or G1: ≤25. log2 and log10 transform it instead (of x + 1 when there are zeros); the answer key then gives the effect per doubling or per 10-fold increase. scale divides it by the number typed in Cuts / scale (e.g. 10 for alcohol in units of 10 g/day, or 1 to undo the scenario’s default unit); the answer key labels the contrast per 10 g/day and re-expresses the true effect in that unit.
Sample size: people in the study (cases plus controls in a case-control study).


Design options, realism and output



Design options: only those of the chosen design are enabled.



Design options: controls per case; follow-up, loss to follow-up and recruitment period for cohorts and trials; subcohort, clusters and ICC, interaction, interim looks, visits and dropout, regions; period and carryover for a crossover; entry threshold for a before-after study; bias, slope and errors of two methods. An empty box keeps the scenario’s value (many scenarios set their own: 4 controls per case, 3 visits); the Study summary lists the values used. Repeated measures gives crossover and longitudinal trials one row per measurement (long, for mixed models) or one per person (wide, for a paired t-test or repeated-measures ANOVA).
Biases builds a bias into the study, and into the answer key’s large study, so the key shows what the biased design estimates: recall bias and controls selected by exposure (case-control), a collider admitted caused by the outcome and the exposure, non-adherence to treatment related to prognosis (a column received; the key adds as-treated and per-protocol rows), informative loss to follow-up, a treatment started during follow-up with no effect (immortal time: treated, treatment_start), and in diagnostic studies spectrum (only the most severe diseased) and partial verification (only some test-negatives get the reference standard). Recall, selection and the collider need a ticked Exposure. See Teaching.



Biases: only those of the chosen design are enabled.


Realism:

missing values in the measured variables: completely at random, depending on the outcome, or depending on the missing value itself (MNAR);
measurement error: the reliability of numeric measures and a share of misclassified categories, non-differential. The answer key uses the same error, so it shows how much the estimates are diluted and how much confounding remains;
data-entry errors (decimal slips, swapped digits, 999 codes) to find and clean, and extra variables with no effect (extra_01, …) for multiple testing and variable selection;
laboratory: values below a marker’s or a biomarker’s detection limit reported as missing, as LOD/2 or as the LOD; diagnostic markers run in batches, optionally with cases and controls in separate batches.




Realism options.


Output: seed and student key (any text, e.g. a student ID: each key gives a different dataset from the same options; capitals and surrounding spaces are ignored), which tables to show, and Answer key report, which saves the whole key (true model, what the design should estimate, markers, diagram, notes) as one HTML page for the teacher. Export class takes the student keys of the class (separated by commas) and saves a zip with one CSV and one codebook per student, a register of keys and seeds, and one answer key report. A teacher code unlocks a library locked with it (see Teaching). CSV files for spreadsheets sets how the CSV files are written: all in UTF-8 with a byte-order mark, so spreadsheets read accented letters; with semicolons and decimal commas when jamovi is in Spanish or Catalan (as Excel expects there), or as chosen.



Several outcomes in one study
Most trials record several outcomes. When the scenario has more than one and the design can carry them (cross-sectional, cohort, prognosis, trial and diagnostic designs), its other outcomes are the first rows of the Variables list, marked outcome in the second column and unticked. Tick the ones to add: they become columns for the same people, they appear in the causal diagram, and the answer key gets a block for each. Outcomes can be linked (correlated beyond their common causes, e.g. HbA1c and control below 7%), and overall survival can be built from a first event (an illness-death model: in the colon cancer trial, death after recurrence).
For example, Intensive blood-pressure control (SPRINT) has five outcomes: the primary cardiovascular event, death from any cause and three harms (acute kidney injury, hypotension, syncope), to weigh benefits against harms and to see what testing many outcomes does. Choose the cardiovascular event as Outcome and tick the other four at the top of the Variables list (time_death, death, kidney_injury, hypotension, syncope are added).



SPRINT with its other outcomes ticked: the answer key has the intervention effect on each outcome.




Two more designs

Before-after (single group): everybody is treated and measured before and after, with no control group. The mean change mixes the effect, the natural trend and, if only people with high values are enrolled (Enrol only above percentile), regression to the mean.
Method comparison: the outcome measured twice in each person, by methods A and B (B with a bias, a proportional bias and its own error), for a Bland-Altman analysis; the key gives the mean difference, the limits of agreement and the regression slope of B on A, attenuated by A’s own error.

The same seed always gives the same study, and the people of the superpopulation do not depend on the design: the same seed under another design samples the same people. Showing the key, the diagram or a table does not draw the study again; only options that change the data do.

Results

Univariate descriptives: mean (SD) and median [IQR], or n (%) per category.


The causal diagram shows the scenario’s structure: measured variables in solid boxes, unmeasured ones dashed, null variables in italics, grey arrows for paths among variables, dark arrows for effects on the outcome. It is shown by default without effect sizes; tick Effect sizes on the diagram to colour the arrows (red raises the outcome, blue lowers it) and give their sizes.

title: Simulated study
text:
The answer key
Answer key adds these parts, for the teacher:

True model: by contrast, the direct (conditional) effects the data were generated with, including the null variables, and the total effect of each variable that also acts through others (mediators), estimated in a large simulated population; a variable acting only through others reads no direct effect; acts through ….



True model: direct and total effects; education acts only through smoking, BMI, blood pressure, HDL and diabetes.


What this design should estimate: crude and adjusted estimates averaged over three large simulated studies with the same design, measured variables, grouping, measurement error and biases (one for matched case-control), with their Monte Carlo uncertainty in a note. This is what a correct analysis of the student’s data should approach. Adjusted (all) adjusts for every measured variable; Adjusted (DAG) adjusts each one only for the measured variables it does not cause, and approaches its True (total). Where the generating measure differs from the design’s (hazard ratios generated, odds ratios estimated by a case-control study) a note says so. Trials with a binary or event outcome add absolute effects: risk per arm, risk difference, NNT, risk ratio, and the marginal next to the conditional odds or hazard ratio. Diagnostic studies add accuracy at a cut-off: sensitivity, specificity and predictive values, true and in the large study.



Absolute effects of a trial: risks, NNT, and the marginal odds ratio closer to 1 than the conditional one.





Expected estimates: the crude coffee effect disappears after adjustment; systolic pressure in quartiles.


Notes: teaching note of the scenario, calibration of the outcome, latent structure and the sources of the parameters.

The Study summary warns when there are fewer than 10 events per parameter of a model adjusted for every measured variable.

title: Simulated study
text:
Compare designs
Simulate ▸ Compare designs takes one scenario and outcome, the measured variables and a sample size, and simulates every ticked design from the same population (same seed and student key); designs that do not fit the outcome are hidden. It shows:



Compare designs: breast cancer with four measured variables, three designs from the same population.



Studies: rows, cases and controls, events, clusters or regions of each one;
Estimates by design: crude and adjusted estimates with their 95% CI next to the true values, and optionally what each design gives in a large study;
a forest plot of the same estimates, one panel per contrast;
the causal diagram, once, because it is the same for every design: what changes between designs is how the population is sampled, not how it works.




Estimates plot: the cohort of 500 women has 10 cases, so its intervals are far wider than the case-control studies’.


Replicate studies per design (next to the sample size) draws that many studies of each design and reports each estimate’s mean, bias, spread (empirical standard error) next to the model’s, power and the coverage of its confidence intervals, with a plot of their sampling distribution.



Replicate studies: 200 parallel and 200 cluster trials of 500 people.


Open dataset stacks all the studies in one dataset with a design column, to analyse them with jamovi’s filters. Typical exercises: a case-control vs a cohort study of a rare cancer (same estimates, very different precision for the same number of people), a parallel vs a crossover trial, an ecological vs an individual-level analysis.

title: studysim: simulated medical studies for teaching
text: studysim is a jamovi module that simulates plausible datasets of medical studies. A student picks a clinical scenario, one of its outcomes, a study design that fits it, a sample size and some realism, and gets a dataset in a new jamovi window. A hidden answer key gives the true parameters and what crude and adjusted analyses of that design should find.

title: studysim: simulated medical studies for teaching
text:
Why simulated studies
Real teaching datasets are few, and they never come with the truth. A simulated study does: confounders, mediators, effect modifiers and null variables are built in, so students can check whether their analysis recovers the effects, see why the crude estimate differs from the adjusted one, and what a design or a missing variable does to the answer. Every student can get a different dataset from the same assignment (a student key), and the teacher can regenerate any of them.

title: Measures and models
text: Every analysis in this guide goes through the same steps. A question (“does smoking cause coronary heart disease, and by how much?”) becomes an estimand: a precise quantity, such as the risk ratio of a 10-year coronary event for smokers against non-smokers with the same age and sex. A design gathers data that can estimate it. A causal diagram says which variables to adjust for. A model turns the data into a number, and the number is interpreted on the scale of the estimand. This page covers the last two steps: the measures epidemiology uses and how the coefficients of its models are read. The next pages cover the designs, the diagrams and mediation (Lash et al. 2021; Hernán and Robins 2020).

title: Measures and models

Measures of frequency

Prevalence mixes how often a condition starts and how long it lasts: in a steady population, prevalence ≈ incidence rate × mean duration. A treatment that keeps patients alive longer raises prevalence. A risk always refers to a period (“10-year risk”), and it requires everyone to be followed for that period or a method that handles censoring (Kaplan-Meier). When another event can prevent the outcome (death from other causes before a cancer relapse), the risk of the outcome is a cumulative incidence in the presence of a competing event. One minus Kaplan-Meier, which censors the competing deaths, overstates it.

Difference measures say how many people are affected, and that is what decisions need. Ratio measures say how strong the association is, and they are usually more stable across populations with different baseline risks. Report both when you can: a risk ratio of 2 means 10 extra cases per 1000 people if the baseline risk is 1%, and 200 if it is 20%.

The odds ratio is not a risk ratio
The odds ratio approaches the risk ratio only when the outcome is rare (Figure 2). A case-control study of a rare disease therefore estimates the risk (or rate) ratio. A cross-sectional study of a common condition analysed with logistic regression reports odds ratios that look much stronger than the prevalence ratios.





















Figure 2: The odds ratio for a fixed risk ratio (dashed lines), by the risk in the unexposed: equal when the outcome is rare, ever larger as it becomes common.





Conditional and marginal: non-collapsibility
The odds ratio and the hazard ratio have a property that surprises many people. Suppose a treatment multiplies the odds by 3 in every subgroup of patients and the subgroups are perfectly balanced between the arms, so nothing is confounded. The odds ratio of the whole trial is still smaller than 3 (Greenland et al. 1999). Risk differences and risk ratios do not behave this way.

The same rules apply to every model:

A coefficient is the effect of its variable with the other variables in the model held fixed. It is a conditional effect. Whether it is the effect you want depends on which variables are in the model: the causal diagram decides that, not the model.
Per unit. A coefficient for age is per year. A hazard ratio of 1.05 per year is 1.0510 = 1.63 per 10 years. Choose units that make sense: per 10 mmHg, per 5 kg/m², per standard deviation.
Per level. A categorical variable gets one coefficient per level, each against the reference level. Changing the reference changes the numbers but not the model.
Log scale. Logistic, Poisson and Cox coefficients are logarithms: exp(β) is the ratio, and effects of several variables multiply. A log-transformed exposure gives the effect per doubling (log2) or per tenfold increase (log10).
Interaction. With a product term X × Z, the coefficient of X is the effect of X when Z is at its reference or zero, and the interaction coefficient is how much that effect changes per unit of Z. If zero is not a meaningful value of Z (a BMI of zero), centre Z first, or the main effects become meaningless. This is the problem studysim’s center: solves in its own scenarios.
The intercept is the outcome (or its log odds or log rate) when every variable is at zero or its reference: rarely of interest, and meaningless without centring.
Categorising a continuous variable loses information and leaves residual confounding within the categories. It is useful for showing a shape (dose response), not for adjustment.
Small numbers. Logistic and Cox models need roughly ten events per parameter; with fewer, coefficients are unstable and biased away from the null (Peduzzi et al. 1996). studysim warns when a study falls short.

title: Measures and models
text:
Effect modification and interaction

Two words, two questions

Effect modification: the effect of an exposure X differs between groups of another variable Z. The effect of BMI on breast cancer is protective before menopause and harmful after it. Z need not cause anything: it describes in whom X acts more strongly.
Interaction: the joint effect of two exposures is not what their separate effects predict. Smoking and asbestos together cause far more lung cancer than the two separately would suggest. Both are causes, and the question is what happens if we act on both.

They are estimated the same way (X within levels of Z, or a product term X × Z), and the words are often used interchangeably. The distinction matters when deciding what to do: a modifier tells you who benefits most from acting on X.


It depends on the scale
Whether an effect “differs” depends on how effects are measured. In this example, exposure X triples the risk both in people without and with a second factor Z:

On the ratio scale there is no modification: the risk ratio is 3 in both groups. On the difference scale there is a great deal: X adds 2 cases per 100 people without Z and 10 per 100 with Z (Figure 3). Whenever two factors both act, no modification on one scale implies modification on the other.





















Figure 3: The same four risks on a difference scale (left) and on a ratio scale (right): no interaction on the multiplicative scale, a strong one on the additive scale.



Logistic and Cox models are multiplicative: their product term tests departure from multiplying the effects. Public health usually cares about the additive scale, because it counts cases: here, removing X prevents five times more cases among people with Z. The relative excess risk due to interaction, RERI = RR11 − RR10 − RR01 + 1, measures additive interaction from ratio measures: here 15 − 3 − 5 + 1 = 8 (0 means no additive interaction).

When the other variable is continuous and zero is meaningless, a main effect is an extrapolation far from the data. Centre the continuous variable first (subtract a typical value), so that the main effect of the modifier holds at that typical value.
Breast cancer risk factors: the effect of BMI is modified by menopause (per 5 kg/m², HR 0.93 before and 1.12 after). The table fits the same interaction model to a large simulated case-control study, with BMI as it is and centred at the population mean.

A modifier that reverses the effect
Dexamethasone in hospitalised COVID-19 (RECOVERY): dexamethasone lowers mortality in patients on oxygen or ventilation, but not in those without respiratory support. This is qualitative modification: the effect changes direction. Its overall odds ratio, averaged over the patients of the trial, would hide both the harm and the largest benefit.





















Figure 5: Odds ratios of death in a simulated RECOVERY trial of 30,000 patients, by respiratory support (dots and 95% CI) and the true values (crosses): harm without support, benefit growing with the severity. The odds ratio of all patients averages them.





In practice

Decide in advance which modifiers to examine and why (biology, previous evidence). Testing many subgroups guarantees false positives.
Report the effect within each group, with its confidence interval, and the test of interaction. A significant effect in one subgroup and a non-significant one in another is not evidence that they differ: compare them with the interaction test.
Interaction tests have little power: detecting an interaction as large as the main effect needs about four times the sample size. A non-significant test does not show that the effect is the same.
Say which scale you used, and give the additive measures (RD, RERI) when the question is about how many cases could be prevented.

title: Direct and indirect effects: mediation
text: An exposure often acts through intermediate variables: obesity raises blood pressure, which raises the risk of a heart attack. Mediation analysis splits the total effect of an exposure into the part that goes through a mediator (the indirect effect) and the rest (the direct effect). The aim is to explain how an exposure works, or what share of its effect an intervention on the mediator could remove. It needs more assumptions than estimating a total effect, and those assumptions are where most mediation analyses fail (VanderWeele 2016; Hernán and Robins 2020).

title: Direct and indirect effects: mediation
text:
Effects to estimate





















Figure 1: Left, the total effect c of X on Y. Right, the same effect split into the path through the mediator M (a, from X to M, and b, from M to Y given X) and the direct path c′ (from X to Y given M).











effect
question
definition




Total effect (TE)
what if X changed?
compares Y with X and without X, M following X


Controlled direct effect (CDE)
what if X changed and M were fixed at a value m for everyone?
depends on m when X and M interact


Natural direct effect (NDE)
what if X changed but M stayed as it would be without X?
the effect not through M


Natural indirect effect (NIE)
what if X stayed, but M changed as X would change it?
the effect through M



On the difference scale TE = NDE + NIE, and the proportion mediated is NIE / TE. In linear models without an X × M interaction the classic approach of Baron and Kenny (Baron and Kenny 1986) gives them directly:

product method: NIE = a × b, NDE = c′;
difference method: NIE = c − c′.

The two agree for linear models of continuous outcomes. For binary and survival outcomes (logistic, Cox) they do not, because odds and hazard ratios are non-collapsible: c − c′ then mixes mediation with the change of scale (Measures and models). With an X × M interaction, or with non-linear models, natural effects need the counterfactual definitions and software that implements them (Imai et al. 2010).

title: Direct and indirect effects: mediation
text:
A checklist

Write the diagram with the exposure, the mediator, the outcome and the confounders of all three pairs (Causal diagrams).
Make sure the mediator happens after the exposure and before the outcome.
Adjust the mediator model for exposure-mediator confounders, and the outcome model for exposure-outcome and mediator-outcome confounders.
Test the exposure × mediator interaction; if present, report controlled direct effects at chosen values of M, or natural effects from software that allows the interaction.
Use bootstrap confidence intervals for indirect effects.
Discuss unmeasured mediator-outcome confounding, which randomising the exposure does not remove, and run a sensitivity analysis.

A scenario in brief
id: breast_cancer_risk
label: {en: Breast cancer risk factors, es: Factores de riesgo de cáncer de mama}
variables:
  age: {from: dictionary, dist: "uniform(35, 75)"}
  menarche: {type: continuous, dist: normal(12.6, 1.4), range: [9, 17], round: 0}
  menopause:
    type: binary
    levels: [pre, post]
    p: plogis((age - 51) / 1.5)          # rule: menopause depends on age
  hrt:
    type: binary
    p: 0.25
    levels: [never, ever]
    only_if: menopause == "post"         # structural value
    otherwise: never
structure:                                 # latent paths among variables
  - [age, parity, 0.25]
outcomes:
  breast_cancer:
    type: event
    rate: 2.5/1000
    designs: [case_control, matched_cc, cohort]
    effects:
      age: {HR: 1.04, per: 1}

null_variables: [education, coffee]
teaching: {en: "Age confounds parity and menopause...", es: "..."}

Variables: continuous (normal, log-normal, gamma, beta, uniform), counts (Poisson, negative binomial), binary, nominal, ordinal and genotypes.
Structure and correlations among variables, and rules: a probability that depends on other variables, structural values (only_if/otherwise) and formulas for derived variables.
Outcomes: binary (prevalence), events (rate, risk or median; Weibull shape), continuous (also on the log scale) and counts, each with conditional effects (OR, HR, RR, ratio, beta), effect modification (by:, centred at the population mean of the variable unless center: says otherwise) and interventions for trials; diagnostic markers with an AUC, a cutoff, a dependence on covariates (depends:) or on disease severity (severity_sd).
Translations: labels in several languages, and an i18n: section with the column names and category labels students see.
A lock: typed in Teacher code before exporting, it locks the exported library; while it is loaded, the answer key, the true values and the effects need the same code (a deterrent: the file itself holds the parameters).

title: Causal diagrams
text: A regression model adjusts for whatever variables it is given, and it cannot tell a confounder from a mediator or a collider. That knowledge comes from outside the data: what causes what, and in what order. A directed acyclic graph (DAG) writes it down, so that the choice of adjustment variables follows from explicit assumptions that others can check and dispute (Greenland et al. 1999; Shrier and Platt 2008; Hernán and Robins 2020).

title: Causal diagrams
text:
Reading a DAG

Each node is a variable; each arrow is a direct causal effect, in the direction of time.
The absence of an arrow is the strong assumption: no direct effect.
Acyclic: no variable causes itself through a loop. A variable measured at several times appears as several nodes.
Every common cause of two variables in the diagram must be in it, measured or not. Unmeasured ones are drawn too (dashed here).
A path is any sequence of arrows, whatever their direction. A causal path from X to Y follows the arrows; a backdoor path starts with an arrow into X.
A collider on a path is a node where two arrowheads meet (→ C ←).

Associations travel along paths. A path is open (it transmits association) unless it contains a collider, or a non-collider that has been adjusted for. Adjusting for a collider opens the path through it.

title: Causal diagrams
section: Building a DAG for a study, step by step
text:
Building a DAG for a study, step by step
The question: what is the effect of body mass index on the 10-year risk of coronary heart disease?

Define the exposure, the outcome and time zero: BMI at entry, a coronary event in 10 years, follow-up from entry.
Add the causes of the outcome you know of, measured or not: age, sex, blood pressure, cholesterol, HDL, diabetes, smoking.
Add the causes of the exposure: age, physical activity; and the causes of those, such as education, which also affects smoking.
Add every common cause of two variables already in the diagram, measured or not. A missing common cause is the most common error.
Order by time, left to right, and decide for each arrow whether it can exist. BMI raises blood pressure, lowers HDL and causes diabetes: those three come after BMI and are mediators of its effect.
Add how people got into the study and how variables were measured, when these could depend on exposure or outcome (selection, missing data, misclassification).
Find the backdoor paths from BMI to coronary disease and a set of measured variables that blocks all of them without containing a descendant of BMI (the backdoor criterion). Software does this: dagitty.net or the R package dagitty (Textor et al. 2016).
Check what you assumed: draw the alternative diagrams that colleagues would defend, and see whether the adjustment set changes.

Age is a confounder, and physical activity (or education) blocks the backdoor path BMI ← activity ← education → smoking → CHD. Sex and cholesterol only affect the outcome (precision variables); coffee is irrelevant.



The backdoor paths from BMI are BMI ← age → … → CHD and BMI ← activity ← education → smoking → CHD. Adjusting for {age, activity} blocks both, and so does {age, education}. Adding sex and cholesterol is harmless. Adding blood pressure, HDL or diabetes is not: they are on the causal path, so the model would estimate only the part of BMI’s effect that does not go through them.

title: Causal diagrams
section: Selection bias is conditioning on a collider
text:
Selection bias is conditioning on a collider





















Figure 11: Selection as a collider (double border: the analysis is restricted to S). Left: hospital patients are admitted for the disease or for other conditions caused by smoking. Right: frail patients drop out more often when treated, and analysing only those followed links treatment and frailty.



Restricting a study to a group of people is conditioning on whatever put them in it. When getting in depends on the exposure and on the outcome (or its causes), the selection node is a collider, and the study finds an association that does not exist in the population (Hernán et al. 2004). The same structure explains biased hospital controls, informative losses to follow-up and analyses of complete cases. studysim builds these on purpose (Biases). Two more problems are diagrammed the same way: measurement error, a measured X* caused by X, and immortal time, a treatment that can only start among those who survive.

title: Causal diagrams
section: Choosing the adjustment set in practice
text:
Choosing the adjustment set in practice
When the full diagram is uncertain, a practical rule (VanderWeele 2019):

Adjust for every measured variable that causes the exposure, the outcome or both (pre-exposure).
Leave out variables known to be instruments (they cause the exposure only).
Add good proxies of unmeasured common causes.
Never adjust for something caused by the exposure (a mediator) when the question is the total effect, nor for consequences of the outcome.

Then check: with how many events per parameter will the model be fitted? A large adjustment set in a small study is unstable (Measures and models). Prefer the smallest valid set, plus strong predictors of the outcome.





















Figure 12: A rough path to an adjustment set for a total effect: variables that precede the exposure and cause it or the outcome are adjusted for, except pure instruments; variables caused by the exposure or by the outcome are not.

title: Causal diagrams
section: Effect modification is not in the diagram
text:
Effect modification is not in the diagram
A DAG shows which variables cause which, not how their effects combine. Two variables with arrows into Y may act additively, multiplicatively or only together, and the diagram looks the same. Effect modification is a feature of the effect of X, reported within levels of the modifier (Measures and models).

title: Observational designs
text: In an observational study the investigator does not decide who is exposed. Exposed and unexposed people may differ in other ways that affect the outcome (confounding), people may enter the study in ways related to exposure and outcome (selection bias), and exposure or outcome may be measured with error (information bias). Each design is a way of sampling a population. The analysis has to match that sampling, and the causal diagram says what to adjust for.

title: Observational designs
text:
Cross-sectional study
What it is. Exposure and outcome measured at the same time in a sample of a population: a health survey, a screening programme.
Estimates. Prevalence, and prevalence ratios or odds ratios between groups.





















Figure 1: Episodes of a disease in a population (one line each). A survey sees only the episodes in progress on its day (bright): the long ones are overrepresented, so a prevalent sample mixes the causes of getting the disease with the causes of keeping it.



Strengths. Quick and cheap; describes the burden of a condition and plans services; studies many exposures and outcomes at once.
Limitations. Exposure and outcome are measured together, so their time order is often unknown (does low activity cause depression, or the reverse?). Prevalent cases over-represent long-lasting disease (Figure 1). Survivors only: people who died of the disease are missing.
Analysis. Prevalence with its confidence interval; logistic regression (odds ratios) or, better for common outcomes, a log-binomial or Poisson model with robust errors (prevalence ratios); linear regression for continuous outcomes.
Interpretation. An odds ratio of 1.8 for diabetes with obesity means the odds of having diabetes are 1.8 times higher in obese people with the same values of the other variables in the model. It is not a risk of developing diabetes, and with a common outcome it overstates the prevalence ratio.
In studysim. Blood pressure in US adults or Diabetes in Pima women, cross-sectional design.

title: Observational designs
text:
Ecological study
What it is. The units are groups (regions, countries, years), with only group summaries: the rate of the outcome, the mean or percentage of the exposure.
Estimates. The association between group summaries. It is not the effect on individuals.





















Figure 2: The ecological fallacy. Across regions (open circles, dashed line) more exposure goes with more of the outcome; within every region (coloured lines) the individual association is the opposite. Something that differs between regions confounds the regional comparison.



Strengths. Uses routine data (registries, censuses), so it is fast and cheap; studies exposures that only exist at group level (policies, water hardness, air pollution); good for generating hypotheses (Morgenstern 1995).
Limitations. The ecological fallacy (Figure 2): a group-level association need not hold for individuals, because regions differ in many things at once (contextual confounding) and nobody knows who in a region was exposed and who fell ill. Group summaries also hide non-linear effects.
Analysis. Regression of the regional rate on regional means and percentages, weighted by population size (Poisson with the population as offset for counts).
Interpretation. A coefficient per percentage point of smokers is the change in the regional rate between regions that differ by one point. It is not the risk ratio of smoking.
In studysim. Water hardness and mortality or Dietary fat and breast cancer, ecological design: compare the regional slope with the individual effect in the answer key.

title: Observational designs
text:
Cohort study
What it is. People free of the outcome are classified by exposure and followed until the outcome, a competing event, loss to follow-up or the end of the study.





















Figure 3: Twenty-six people of a simulated cohort (Coronary heart disease incidence), each followed from entry: a cross is a coronary event, a bar the end of follow-up without one (loss or end of the study).



Estimates. Risks (cumulative incidence), rates and hazards in each exposure group, and their ratios and differences.
Strengths. Exposure is measured before the outcome, so the time order is clear and recall cannot be biased by the outcome; several outcomes of one exposure can be studied; it gives absolute risks.
Limitations. Large and long for rare or slow outcomes (the coronary cohort of 3,000 people has about 250 events in 10 years); losses to follow-up that depend on prognosis bias the results (informative censoring); confounding, as in any observational design; exposure can change during follow-up.
Analysis. Kaplan-Meier curves and the log-rank test; Cox regression for hazard ratios adjusted for confounders; Poisson regression of counts with log person-time as offset for rates; logistic regression only when everybody is followed for the same period.
Interpretation. A hazard ratio of 1.6 for smoking means that at any time during follow-up, among those still free of the event, smokers have 1.6 times the event rate of non-smokers with the same values of the adjustment variables. It assumes the ratio is constant over time (check proportional hazards).
Two traps. A treatment that starts during follow-up must not be analysed as if it were present from entry: the treated had to survive until they started it (immortal time), and the treatment looks protective even when useless (Suissa 2008). Treat it as a time-dependent variable, or compare from a landmark time. And adjusting for something that happens after the exposure (a mediator, or a consequence of the outcome) changes the question; see Causal diagrams.
In studysim. Coronary heart disease incidence, cohort; Biases ▸ Informative loss to follow-up and Treatment started during follow-up.

Prognosis and competing risks
A prognosis study is a cohort of patients from diagnosis or treatment, recruited over several years (staggered entry), to describe survival and its predictors. When patients can die of something else before the outcome of interest, that death is a competing event. A Cox model that censors it estimates the cause-specific hazard ratio, a valid measure of the effect on the rate of the event. But 1 − Kaplan-Meier, which treats the deaths from other causes as if those patients could still have the event, overstates its cumulative incidence (Figure 4).





















Figure 4: Deaths from breast cancer in a simulated prognosis cohort with deaths from other causes (Breast cancer prognosis). 1 − Kaplan-Meier overstates the proportion who die of breast cancer, and the more so the more patients die of something else first.

title: Observational designs
text:
Case-control study
What it is. All (or a random sample of) the cases of a disease arising in a source population, and a sample of people from the same population who are not cases (controls); exposure is then measured in both, usually looking back.





















Figure 5: A case-control study samples by outcome: all the cases (red) of the source population and a random sample of the non-cases. The proportion of cases in the study is set by the design, so it estimates odds ratios, not risks.



Estimates. The exposure odds ratio, which equals the disease odds ratio. With controls sampled from those still at risk when each case occurs (risk-set sampling, as in a nested case-control study) it estimates the rate ratio, with no rare-disease assumption. Otherwise it approximates the risk ratio when the disease is rare.
Strengths. Efficient for rare diseases and long latencies (a few hundred cases instead of a cohort of a hundred thousand); many exposures can be studied for one disease; fast.
Limitations. Controls must come from the population that gave rise to the cases: hospital controls admitted for diseases related to the exposure distort the odds ratio (selection bias). Exposure recalled after the diagnosis can be reported differently by cases (recall bias). No absolute risks unless the sampling fractions are known.
Analysis. Logistic regression with case status as the outcome, adjusted for confounders. The intercept is meaningless (it reflects the sampling), but the odds ratios are valid.
Interpretation. An odds ratio of 7.7 for smoking 1-14 cigarettes a day means the odds of lung cancer are 7.7 times higher than in never smokers with the same age and sex. For a rare disease it reads as the rate ratio.
In studysim. Lung cancer and smoking or Oesophageal cancer, case-control; Biases ▸ Recall bias and Controls selected by exposure, ticking smoking as the exposure.

Matched case-control
Each case gets controls with the same values of some confounders (age, sex, hospital). Matching makes the groups comparable on those variables and can increase efficiency, but it must be kept in the analysis: conditional logistic regression compares each case with its own controls. An ordinary logistic regression of matched data is biased towards the null, the effect of a matching variable cannot be estimated, and matching on something caused by the exposure (overmatching) removes part of the effect.


Nested case-control and case-cohort
Both sample a cohort whose follow-up is already recorded, to avoid measuring an expensive exposure (a biomarker in stored blood) on everybody.





















Figure 6: Nested case-control: for each case (here the highlighted one), controls are drawn from its risk set, the people still followed and free of the event at the case’s event time (lines crossing the dashed line). A control can later become a case.




Nested case-control: for each case, a few controls from its risk set (Figure 6). Analysed with conditional logistic regression on the risk sets, it estimates the hazard ratio of the full cohort.
Case-cohort (PRENTICE 1986): a random subcohort chosen at the start, plus every case. The same subcohort serves several outcomes. The analysis is a Cox model weighted for the sampling (Prentice or Lin-Ying weights) with a robust variance; it estimates the hazard ratio.

In studysim. Relapse of Wilms tumour: nested case-control and case-cohort from the same cohort.

What it estimates

the marginal distribution of each variable (normal, log-normal, gamma or uniform; Poisson or negative binomial for counts; category proportions);
the latent correlations, by inverting the Gaussian copula the simulator uses, so a simulated study reproduces the observed correlations;
the conditional effects on the outcome (logistic, linear, Poisson or Cox, with 95% CI and the crude estimate), and the prevalence, mean, risk or Weibull shape that calibrates it.

Check by simulating analyses one large study simulated from the derived scenario with the same model: the Re-estimated column should match the adjusted estimates.

Missing values in the variables chooses how the outcome model deals with rows that miss a covariate (the distributions and correlations always use every observed value, and the outcome targets every row with the outcome):

Values that do not apply
Real datasets record some variables only for some people: the age at first oral contraceptive use is blank for women who never used them, the years of use are 0, the age at the first smear test is coded 99 when there was none. Before estimating anything, Derive:

reads an all-nines value at the top of a variable’s range (99, 999), far more frequent than the values just below it, as missing, and so a 0 far below every other value (a blood pressure or a BMI of 0 that meant “not measured”, as in the Pima data);
finds variables that are missing, or one constant, in a level of another variable and observed elsewhere (structural values). The scenario writes them with only_if/otherwise (e.g. only_if: co == "sí", otherwise: 0), their distribution comes from the people they apply to, their correlations with that variable are left out (it is a rule), and the model gives the other rows the otherwise value, so no rows are lost: the effect of the variable is among those it applies to, and the effect of the other variable is at the otherwise value;
reports pairs of numbers whose order the data never break (start age ≤ end age ≤ age): the scenario cannot keep such an order, so write one from the other with a formula or leave one out.

Columns that jamovi read as nominal but hold numbers (integers from a CSV) are read as numbers. Try it with chd_sim.csv, a simulated cohort.

title: Derive a scenario from data
text:
Finishing it with an AI
The data cannot tell causes from correlates, so a derived scenario has undirected correlations and raw column names. Export scenario writes it as YAML with a derivation: block (source, original names, missing data, estimates and correlations), which is what an AI needs to finish it:

A prompt for any AI: attach the exported YAML and schema.md. It returns the scenario with names and translations, a causal structure, rules for impossible combinations, rounded effects, a teaching note and references marked to verify, plus a report of its decisions.
A Claude skill (also as a zip in the Releases): the same steps, with a validator, check_scenario.R, that checks the file, simulates a large study and compares the re-estimated effects with the data’s, following renamed variables and changed reference categories.

Review the result before teaching with it: the causal structure is a judgement, and references must be checked.

text:
Simulating many studies
Compare designs with Replicate studies per design draws hundreds of studies of each design and reports, for each estimate, its mean, bias, spread (the standard error a study does not see), power and the coverage of its confidence intervals: chance and bias side by side.

title: How it works
text:
Covariates come from a Gaussian copula structured as a DAG: every variable has a latent standard normal; those without parents are jointly normal with the scenario’s correlations, the others are linear in their parents’ latents (standardised path coefficients) plus noise. Each latent is mapped to its marginal by the quantile function (NORTA): exact marginals (truncated to their range if given) with the intended dependence. Rules then tie variables together: probabilities that depend on other variables, structural values and formulas.
People are generated in chunks of 5000 with seeds derived from the seed, the scenario and the chunk, so person k is the same whatever the design or the sample size, and a student key changes the seed.

title: How it works
text:
Outcomes and calibration

binary: logistic model; events: Weibull proportional hazards (inverse transform); continuous: linear (optionally on the log scale); counts: Poisson or negative binomial.
The intercept, or the baseline hazard, is calibrated on 100 000 simulated people so the population has the scenario’s prevalence, rate, risk at a time, median or mean.
Each person has their own outcome noise, shared by their treated and untreated versions, so trials compare potential outcomes of the same people.
A numeric effect modified by another variable (by:) acts on its distance to a center (the population mean by default), so the modifier has no implied effect of its own; a continuous outcome with a range is drawn from the truncated distribution.

title: How it works
text:
The answer key
The true model lists the direct effects used. The total effect of a variable that acts through others (its descendants in the structure and the rules) is the regression of the outcome on the variable and on every variable it does not cause, in a simulated population of 40 000 to 200 000 people: a valid adjustment set of the diagram, which leaves the mediators out. Where nothing the variable causes acts on the outcome, the total effect is the direct one.
The expected estimates are the average of three large studies of the same design (one for matched case-control, whose matching is slow): 40 000 rows, more for a rare outcome so that each has about 5000 events, up to 300 000; 1500–3000 cases for case-control designs; 200 regions for an ecological study. Each is analysed with the model a student would fit: logistic, conditional logistic, Cox, linear (with subject effects in a crossover, a mixed model for a longitudinal trial) or Poisson; crude for each variable, adjusted for all measured ones, and adjusted for the measured variables each one does not cause (Adjusted (DAG)). Ratios are averaged on the log scale; the note under the table gives the Monte Carlo uncertainty of the average.
Trials’ absolute effects come from the potential outcomes of 100 000 people under every arm; diagnostic accuracy at a cut-off is true in a clean population of 100 000 and expected in a large study with the same biases.

Each kind of variable, worked
Small studies, one per kind of variable (two for confounders), each simulated with a few lines of code so that the true effect is known exactly. The outcome is always a continuous measure analysed with linear regression, so the estimates are easy to compare: a coefficient is the change in the outcome per unit of the exposure. Each table gives the true effect, the crude estimate and the estimate adjusted for the third variable, with 95% confidence intervals.

1. Confounder: coffee, smoking and blood pressure
Smokers drink more coffee, and smoking raises blood pressure. Coffee itself has no effect.

1b. Negative confounding: salt, age and blood pressure
Confounding does not always create an effect; it can also hide one. Salt raises blood pressure (+2 mmHg per g/day), and so does age (+0.45 mmHg per year). But younger people eat more salt, so people with a high salt intake are younger and, for that reason alone, have lower blood pressure.

What adjusting does: the crude analysis finds no effect of salt at all; adjusting for age reveals it. The direction of confounding bias is the product of the signs of the confounder’s two arrows: here (age → salt: −) × (age → blood pressure: +) = −, so the crude estimate is pulled down, towards zero or past it. Two positive or two negative arrows exaggerate an effect (as smoking did for coffee); opposite signs mask it. A null crude association is therefore no reason to drop an exposure before adjusting.


2. Mediator: exercise, body mass index and blood pressure
Exercise lowers blood pressure directly (−1 mmHg per hour a week) and by lowering BMI (−0.8 kg/m² per hour, each kg/m² adding 1.2 mmHg). Its total effect is −1 + (−0.8 × 1.2) = −1.96 mmHg per hour.
